summary: Defines Connectivity Verification types that use Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) together with Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification (VCCV). VCCV gives a pseudowire a control channel for operations and management checks, and BFD is used over that channel to verify the connection is alive.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC lets two ends of a pseudowire use BFD messages to check whether the connection is working. The endpoints choose one of four message types based on how the messages are carried and whether they also report fault status.

which udp port does bfd use for pseudowires
how is a bfd cv type selected
subtitle: BFD connectivity checks for pseudowires using the VCCV control channel.

tldr.problem: A pseudowire needs a way to detect data-plane failures and, in some cases, communicate fault status between its endpoints.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four BFD connectivity-verification types: two encapsulations, each with fault-detection-only and fault-detection-plus-status options. Both ends run one asynchronous BFD session per pseudowire.
tldr.outcome: The endpoints select one common type and keep using it until the pseudowire is re-signaled. RFC 5885 has been updated by RFC 6478 and RFC 7885.

today: RFC 5885 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6478 and RFC 7885.

sections.title: BFD over a Pseudowire Control Channel
sections.content:
Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification (VCCV) provides a control channel associated with a pseudowire (PW), along with operations and management functions. This RFC defines Connectivity Verification (CV) types that carry Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) over that channel.

BFD primarily detects data-plane failures on the PW. Some types can also carry fault status between endpoints, which may be translated into status codes used by access technologies. The specification covers single-segment pseudowires and BFD asynchronous mode over Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) and Layer Two Tunneling Protocol version 3 (L2TPv3) pseudowires.
sections.plainLanguage: BFD sends control messages over a pseudowire's VCCV channel so its endpoints can detect failures. Some message types can also carry fault status.

sections.title: Four BFD Connectivity-Verification Types
sections.content:
The four BFD CV types combine two encapsulations with two functions. Types 0x04 and 0x08 use IP and UDP headers; types 0x10 and 0x20 carry BFD directly after the PW Associated Channel Header (PW-ACH).

Within each encapsulation, the lower type provides fault detection only, while the other provides fault detection and attachment-circuit or pseudowire fault-status signaling. The same four values are defined for MPLS and L2TPv3 pseudowires.
sections.plainLanguage: The types differ in two ways: whether BFD uses IP/UDP headers, and whether it also carries fault status. Each type combines one choice from each category.

sections.title: How the BFD Session Runs
sections.content:
Both endpoints must agree on the BFD CV type. A statically provisioned PW uses the type configured at both ends; a dynamically established PW signals that both ends support BFD on its control channel.

There is one BFD session per pseudowire. Both endpoints act as Active and send initial BFD Control packets. The PW demultiplexer provides enough context to associate the first packet with the session, so the endpoints do not exchange discriminators. BFD must run in asynchronous mode, and both endpoints must send messages.

If an endpoint misses the configured number of BFD intervals, it declares its receive direction down and signals the state to its peer. The peer can then declare its transmit direction down.
sections.plainLanguage: Both endpoints send BFD messages over the control channel. If one endpoint misses enough messages, it declares the connection down in that direction and informs the other endpoint.

sections.title: IP/UDP and PW-ACH Encapsulation
sections.content:
With IP/UDP encapsulation, BFD Control packets use UDP destination port 3784 and a source port from 49152 through 65535. The TTL or Hop Limit is 255 under the referenced Generalized TTL Security procedures. This form can coexist with other IP-based VCCV checks.

With PW-ACH encapsulation, a raw BFD Control packet follows the PW-ACH without IP/UDP headers. The pseudowire must use the PW-ACH control-word format, and its Channel Type must be 0x0007. A pseudowire without a suitable control word or L2-specific sublayer must not use the PW-ACH BFD types.

The RFC registers the four CV type values and the PW-ACH Channel Type.
sections.plainLanguage: BFD can travel inside IP/UDP headers or directly after a PW-ACH header. The direct form requires a pseudowire format that provides that channel header.

sections.title: Selecting One Common Type
sections.content:
For dynamically established pseudowires, only types advertised by both endpoints are available. If they share more than one type, the RFC's precedence order is 0x20, 0x10, 0x08, then 0x04.

Types 0x08 and 0x20 should not be used when another control protocol can already signal attachment-circuit or pseudowire status. Once an endpoint has selected a type, it must keep using that type until the PW is re-signaled. Changing type requires tearing down and re-establishing the PW.
sections.plainLanguage: The endpoints choose the highest-precedence type that both advertised. They keep that choice until the pseudowire is taken down and established again.

sections.title: Congestion Considerations
sections.content:
BFD sends fixed-size packets at intervals configured by its minimum transmit and receive settings. Its bandwidth use is therefore limited by configuration. This is sufficient when the configured BFD rate is small compared with the pseudowire rate; otherwise, BFD needs an adaptive congestion-control mechanism.

The VCCV channel must not rate-limit traffic below the maximum configurable BFD bandwidth. It should not add a congestion-control loop that interferes with BFD's own behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: BFD's configured intervals determine how much bandwidth its messages use. The VCCV channel must leave enough capacity for that configured rate.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says its BFD CV types introduce no additional security issues beyond those in RFC 5085, RFC 5880, and RFC 5881. IP/UDP-encapsulated BFD uses the TTL and Hop Limit procedures from RFC 5881, including the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC relies on the existing VCCV and BFD security considerations. Its IP/UDP form also uses TTL and Hop Limit checks described by the single-hop BFD specification.
